options: A single Oracle Fusion screen for entering sales orders
A report that lists overdue invoices only
The business process from a customer's order through fulfillment, billing, and collecting cash
The approval workflow for purchase orders
questions.explain: O2C is the end-to-end business process: order, fulfillment, billing, collection, and the accounting that results.

questions.q: Put these in the order a single sales order typically moves through them.
options: Order Management, Shipping, Receivables, Cash Management
Receivables, Order Management, Shipping, Cash Management
Shipping, Cash Management, Order Management, Receivables
Cash Management, Receivables, Shipping, Order Management
questions.explain: The order is captured in Order Management, fulfilled by Shipping, billed by Receivables, then collected by Cash Management.

questions.q: Why is Order-to-Cash described as a cycle rather than a one-way transaction?
options: Because every order must be entered twice
Because invoices expire and must be recreated
Because Oracle requires orders to be re-approved every 30 days
Because outcomes from one order, like payment history, affect decisions on future orders
questions.explain: A customer's payment behavior on past orders feeds forward into credit checks and risk decisions on future orders — it loops.

questions.q: This course assumes you already understand which prior topics?
options: Nothing — it starts from zero accounting knowledge
General Ledger, Accounts Payable, and Accounts Receivable basics
Only Salesforce administration
Python and SQL scripting
questions.explain: This course builds on GL, AP, and AR, which earlier courses in the path already cover, and does not re-teach them from scratch.

questions.q: What is the main new piece this course adds that the Receivables course did not cover?
options: How to set up a supplier site
How to configure a chart of accounts
Order Management — the module that decides what gets invoiced in the first place
Fixed asset depreciation methods
questions.explain: Receivables covers invoicing and cash once a transaction exists. Order Management is what creates the transaction that gets billed.
